teaching_gems.gem: Frame embedding as two opposite tasks: shape to metric (induced metric) and metric to shape (embedding diagram), doing the easy direction first.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Learners build confidence computing metrics of familiar shapes before facing the underdetermined inverse problem, and they see the same formula used both ways.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Two-way toggle: 'I have a surface' (pick a shape, get ds^2) versus 'I have a metric' (type ds^2, the app searches for a surface of revolution), sharing one 3D viewport.

teaching_gems.gem: Solve the same object by two independent methods and require the answers to agree, reconciling different-looking results with a coordinate substitution.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Agreement is a self-check, and the reconciliation step (r = sin theta) teaches that metrics are only defined up to coordinate changes.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Side-by-side derivation panes for method I and II with a substitution slider that morphs one line element into the other symbol by symbol.

teaching_gems.gem: Choose the angular embedding functions so the circumference condition is automatic, reducing embedding to a single ODE for the height profile.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Symmetry turns a scary PDE problem into integration, and the same trick handles wormholes, spheres and hyperbolic surfaces.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Profile builder: user specifies R(u) and g_uu; the app integrates dZ/du live, draws the surface of revolution and shades red where no real slope exists.

teaching_gems.gem: Stage a deliberate failure: show the hyperbolic metric needs an imaginary slope before explaining why and how to escape.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A visible contradiction is memorable and motivates both partial embeddings and a change of ambient signature.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Length-budget bar: for each chi, a bar shows the radial length allowed by the metric versus the horizontal length already used by the circumference; the vertical slope is the leftover, which goes negative for sinh-form metrics.

teaching_gems.gem: Rescue a failed embedding by flipping one sign in the host metric, so the hyperbolic plane becomes an ordinary-looking hyperboloid.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Shows students that 'flat space' can have indefinite signature and connects hyperbolic geometry to Minkowski velocity space and cosmology.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Sign switch on the ambient metric: with + the hyperboloid's measured arc lengths mismatch the target metric; with - they match, displayed as a live residual.

teaching_gems.gem: Use two topologically equivalent drawings of the same wormhole to separate local geometry from global topology.
teaching_gems.why_effective: The comparison is visual and immediate, and it inoculates against assuming a metric determines connectivity.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Morphing animation between folded-sheet and handle views with fixed throat metric and a topology selector including disconnected universes.

teaching_gems.gem: Warn explicitly that a sphere-like line element on the one-sheet hyperboloid does not make it a sphere, checking coordinate ranges against the defining equation.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Trains the habit of checking domains and signs, not just formula shapes.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Formula-matching quiz where each candidate surface's r-range and sign of g_rr must be set before the app accepts a match.

teaching_gems.gem: Partial embedding plus Minding's theorem: embed a band of a constant-negative-curvature surface and argue it represents hyperbolic geometry locally.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Gives a tangible 3D object for negative curvature and introduces local isometry without heavy machinery.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Interactive collar surface for d chi^2 + cosh^2 chi d phi^2 that grows until chi = arcsinh 1, with patches that can be dragged onto a Poincaré disc to show local match.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The opening says an embedding needs more than one extra dimension, yet the 2-sphere embeds in R^3 with exactly one extra; the intended claim is presumably 'at least one', and in general many more may be needed.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Confusion about dimension counting and about why the hyperbolic plane fails in R^3.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State: at least one extra dimension is needed; D + 1 suffices for some spaces (spheres) but not all; Nash guarantees some finite N.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Footnote 2 says any Riemannian manifold can be embedded in Euclidean space, while the text later says some surfaces cannot be embedded in Euclidean space.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Qualify both: embedding in R^3 can fail (hyperbolic plane), but higher-dimensional Euclidean embeddings always exist.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: 'This embedding is indeed impossible' follows only from the failure of one rotationally symmetric ansatz; the general impossibility (Hilbert's theorem for the complete hyperbolic plane in R^3) is neither proved nor named.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think any failed guess proves impossibility.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Name Hilbert's theorem, explain the length-budget intuition, and note pieces embed (Exercise D.4, the pseudosphere).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The Example D.2 metric is never identified as the constant-time equatorial slice of the Schwarzschild geometry, and r_S is just called a constant length.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers miss the connection to black holes and Flamm's paraboloid (only named in Exercise 23.5).
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Derive it from the Schwarzschild metric with dt = 0 and theta = pi/2, and name Flamm's paraboloid.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The text says the revolved profile 'generates the spacetime' and calls the sheets flat spacetime, although the picture is of a 2D spatial slice.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Reinforces confusion between space and spacetime pictures and the rubber-sheet misconception.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Say 'spatial slice' explicitly, stress that time is suppressed and that the vertical axis has no physical meaning.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The wormhole is described as a potential shortcut or route to another universe without saying that the Schwarzschild bridge is not traversable.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners leave with a science-fiction impression that Chapter 27 later has to undo.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add a note that no timelike path crosses the Schwarzschild throat (GA ch27 §27.2) and that traversable wormholes need negative energy.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The induced metric of the one-sheet hyperboloid is Lorentzian (2D de Sitter), but the book presents its r-form as 'simply the metric for the 2-sphere' without mentioning signature.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think the formal match is real and miss the de Sitter connection used in Chapters 18, 19 and 49.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Point out r >= 1 makes the dr^2 coefficient negative, and identify the surface as 2D de Sitter spacetime with chi as time.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Symbol slips: D.4 cites D.1 rather than D.2; D.15 has a stray '= sin^2 theta' on its first line; D.18's derivation writes X = r cos theta but the result uses phi; D.20 differentiates with respect to theta while the component is g_phi phi.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Beginners tracking indices lose confidence or copy the errors.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use phi consistently for the azimuth and reference the N-dimensional D.2.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Method II's square-root elimination (Y = +sqrt(a^2 - X^2), Z = +sqrt(1 - X^2 - Y^2)) covers only one branch, and the coordinate X is singular at the ends; the book does not comment.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think method II describes the whole circle or sphere.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Highlight the branch covered and the coordinate singularity where the graph becomes vertical.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Fig. D.4 draws the far regions as literally flat planes and exaggerates the tube length; the true profile keeps rising as sqrt(r) with slope tending to zero.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Misleading intuition about how quickly the geometry becomes flat.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Render the exact profile to scale alongside the stylized sketch.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Exercise D.4 calls the space 'hyperbolic spacetime' and presents Minding's theorem without stressing it is local; the cosh-form metric with periodic phi is a hyperbolic annulus, not globally the hyperbolic plane.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Blurs space versus spacetime and local versus global geometry, just after the book emphasised topology.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Say 'space', and add that equal constant curvature guarantees local, not global, equivalence.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Exercise D.3 supplies the torus as an implicit equation but asks for method I, leaving the parametrization to the reader; Appendix E's answer prints a dv^2 instead of a^2 dv^2.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Stuck students or wrong answers accepted as correct.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Give the parametrization as a hint and correct the printed answer.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Gaussian curvature of the embedded examples is never computed, so the link between embedding shape and intrinsic curvature (positive sphere, negative hyperboloid, both signs on a torus, negative Flamm paraboloid) is left implicit.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Embedding feels like pure drawing rather than a window on curvature.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add K = -f''/f for metrics d chi^2 + f^2 d phi^2 and tabulate K for each example; point to GA ch30.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The one-bullet chapter summary omits the induced-metric recipes, the pseudo-Euclidean fix and the topology caveat.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Revision from the summary alone misses most of the content.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use a fuller summary: two methods, reverse problem, failure in R^3, hyperboloids, geometry versus topology.

tutor_notes: Open with: 'How do you know a bowl is curved, and how would a beetle that can never leave it find out?' Then ask whether spacetime has a 'bowl' around it; steer to the idea that embeddings are pictures, not physics.
Teach method I first with the circle: have the learner write X(theta), Y(theta), differentiate, and sum squares before showing the general formula D.5; then generalize to the sphere.
Check understanding by asking the learner to predict g_theta phi for the sphere before computing it, and to explain why it vanishes (orthogonal coordinate lines).

When method II gives dr^2/(1 - r^2) + r^2 d phi^2, pause and ask 'is this a different surface?' Let them find r = sin theta themselves; mention this exact form reappears for the closed universe in Chapter 16.
For the wormhole, first tell the learner it is the Schwarzschild spatial slice at fixed time in the equatorial plane; then set up the surface-of-revolution ansatz and let them solve for Z(r).

Immediately after the wormhole picture, ask 'what does the vertical direction represent?' Correct answer: nothing physical, only distances along the surface matter. Follow with 'can you travel through it?' and point to Chapter 27 for why not.
Use Fig. D.5 to separate geometry from topology with a simpler example first: a flat sheet versus a cylinder have the same local metric but different connectivity.
Before showing D.25, ask the learner to compute how much radial length the horizontal motion alone uses when the circle radius is sinh chi; the length-budget argument makes the failure intuitive.

When introducing dX^2 + dY^2 - dW^2, connect it to Minkowski space with W as time and the book's (-,+,+,+) signature; ask why the upper hyperboloid sheet is a natural home for hyperbolic geometry (all its tangents are spacelike).
For the one-sheet hyperboloid, insist on checking the range r >= 1 and the sign of the dr^2 coefficient; reveal it is 2D de Sitter spacetime if the learner is heading toward cosmology.

Common learner questions: 'Does spacetime really live in higher dimensions?' (no evidence; Kaluza-Klein and string ideas in Chapters 48-49 are separate speculation); 'Why not always embed in more dimensions?' (possible by Nash, but pictures stop being drawable); 'Is Flamm's paraboloid a picture of gravity pulling things down?' (no: it shows only spatial geometry at fixed time, and the Appendix E answer to Exercise 23.5, citing Zee, warns that such slices mislead about the origin of gravitational effects).
Pace: novices can do Examples D.1 and D.2 in one sitting; hold Examples D.3-D.4 and Exercises D.4-D.5 for learners comfortable with hyperbolic functions and Minkowski signature.
